title: Framing an open question
objectives: Turn "predict tomorrow's futures price" into a target, a horizon and a loss.

screens.title: The open question
screens.prose: About three minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. The interviewer says: "Predict tomorrow's index futures price." The chart is the file we will use.

state.caption: 1,000 daily closes of an index future.

screens.question: Which target will you model?

options.text: The next-day return: a change comparable across days
Tomorrow's close, since that is the number asked for
options.why: You modelled the level. Yesterday's close already predicts it almost perfectly, so the score says little.

options.text: Up or down tomorrow, as a simple yes or no answer
options.why: You threw away the size of the move, and the size decides the profit.

options.text: The 20-day moving average of the close price
options.why: You chose a smoothed series. Tomorrow's price does not follow it.

A price level wanders, so a model of it is easy to score well and hard to learn from.
The return is the change from one close to the next. Model that.

feedback.correct: The next-day return. We still have to say the horizon and the loss.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick a target that is comparable from day to day.

byKey.level: You modelled the price level. A level carries its own past, so almost any lag predicts it.
byKey.dir: You kept only the sign. The profit depends on how far it moves too.
byKey.avg: You modelled a smooth average, which is not the number asked for.

explain.text: The thing to predict is the change, not the level. We name it next, then score it.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def framing(path):
    c = pd.read_csv(path)['close'].to_numpy(float)
    r = np.diff(np.log(c))
    r2_price = np.corrcoef(c[:-1], c[1:])[0, 1] ** 2
    r2_return = np.corrcoef(r[:-1], r[1:])[0, 1] ** 2
    rmse_price = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.diff(c) ** 2))
    rmse_zero = np.sqrt(np.mean(r ** 2))
    return r2_price, r2_return, rmse_price, rmse_zero

hints.text: Returns first: `np.diff(np.log(c))`.
R² of a one-variable line is the squared correlation of the pairs.
Pair `c[:-1]` with `c[1:]`, then do the same for the returns. The miss of "tomorrow = today" is the root mean square of `np.diff(c)`.

feedback.correct: R² of 0.9944 on prices, 0.0153 on returns. "Tomorrow equals today" misses by 57.78 points.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Use log returns and pair each day with the day before.

explain.text: The price model scores 0.9944 and the return model 0.0153, on the same days. A 57.78-point miss on a mean close of 5,561.9 is the baseline any price model must beat.

screens.title: How far ahead
screens.prose: Say daily returns are independent with a standard deviation of 1%. The bars show three horizons. A month of trading is 21 days.
screens.question: What is the 21-day standard deviation, in %?

hints.text: Compare the five-day bar with the one-day bar.
Over five days the spread is $\sqrt{5} = 2.236$ times the daily one.
$\sqrt{21} = 4.583$, so the bar is 4.583.

feedback.correct: 4.583%. Spread grows with the square root of the days.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Variances add over independent days; standard deviations do not.

byKey.linear: You multiplied by 21. That adds the standard deviations, which ignores that good and bad days cancel.
byKey.daily: That is one day. The spread over 21 days is larger.

explain.text: Independent days add their variances, so 21 days have 21 times the variance and $\sqrt{21}$ times the spread. A year of 252 days reaches 15.87%.

screens.title: Three ways to score
screens.prose: A forecast is scored, so choose the score. These are three forecasts and what happened, in %. Go long one unit when the forecast is positive and short one unit when it is negative.
screens.question: Fill in the three scores.

hints.text: Do the errors first: actual minus forecast on each day.
Squares are 0.09, 0.04 and 0.25. A hit means the signs agree.
Mean squared error is 0.38 / 3. One hit in three. Profit is 0.5 - 0.1 - 0.2.

feedback.correct: 0.1267, one hit in three, and a profit of 0.2%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each error and average; count the days the signs agree; sum sign times actual.

explain.text: The same forecasts look poor by hit rate and fair by profit, because day 1 was large and right. The score you choose decides which model wins.

screens.title: A high R²
screens.prose: Each dot is one day: today's close against tomorrow's. A line through all 999 pairs has R² of 0.994. A colleague says the model works.

state.caption: Every 25th day. The line has R² = 0.994 on all 999 pairs.

screens.question: What does the 0.994 tell you?

options.text: Only that prices persist: copying today scores almost as well
It works: 99% of tomorrow's price is explained by what we know today
options.why: You read R² as skill. A level carries its own past, so R² is high for any slow series.

options.text: It is too good to be true, so the data must have leaked
options.why: No leak is needed. Any lagged price predicts a price level this well.

options.text: It would be higher still if we modelled returns instead
options.why: The return version scores 0.015, because returns hardly persist.

hints.text: Draw the line y = x on the cloud.
The dots hug it, so yesterday alone predicts today.
A model that merely copies yesterday gets nearly the same R², so the score measures persistence.

feedback.correct: Persistence, not skill. Judge a model against "tomorrow equals today".
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a model that only copies yesterday would score.

byKey.works: You read R² as skill. Copying yesterday would score nearly the same.
byKey.leak: You looked for a leak. The score is high without one.
byKey.more: You expected returns to score higher. They score 0.015.

explain.text: Copying yesterday scores almost as well, so R² of 0.994 shows only that the series wanders slowly. The honest score is the miss against that baseline.

screens.title: Percentages do not add
screens.prose: A price rises 10% on day 1 and falls 10% on day 2. The simple returns add to zero, yet the price ends at 99.
screens.question: Add the two log returns. What is the two-day log return, in %?

hints.text: Take the log of each growth factor, 1.1 and 0.9.
Their sum is $-0.0101$, which is $\ln 0.99$.

feedback.correct: -1.005%. Log returns add, so the sum matches the price.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take $\ln$ of 1.1 and of 0.9, then add.

byKey.simple: You added the percentages. Simple returns do not add over two days.
byKey.flip: You got the sign wrong. The price ended lower.

explain.text: The log return over any stretch is the sum of the daily log returns, and equals $\ln(P_{end}/P_{start})$. Percentages compound instead, so adding them drifts.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose: A framing has a target $y_{t+1} = \ln(P_{t+1}/P_t)$, a horizon $h$ fixed when you decide, and a loss $L$. The yardstick is the score $L(\text{zero})$ of the dumbest forecast. Say it in three sentences.
screens.question: Which opening would you say?

options.text: Next-day return, decided at the close, scored by profit after costs against zero.
I would regress tomorrow's price on yesterday's price and report the R squared.
options.why: You modelled the level, so the score is persistence.

options.text: I would use the model with the highest R squared over all 1,000 days.
options.why: You scored on the days you fitted. That rewards overfitting.

options.text: I would classify up or down and report the accuracy.
options.why: Accuracy ignores the size of each move and the cost of trading it.

hints.text: Look for a target, a horizon and a loss in one sentence.
The right opening also names what you compare against.
Only one option states all of them.

feedback.correct: Target, horizon, loss and baseline in one breath.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the opening that names all four.

byKey.price: You named the level. The score will be high for free.
byKey.fit: You named no horizon and scored in sample.
byKey.acc: You named a score that ignores size and costs.

explain.text: Say the target, the horizon, the loss and the baseline, in that order. Everything later in the conversation hangs on them.

screens.title: Why the square root
screens.prose: Take $h$ independent daily log returns, each with variance $\sigma^2$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: The $h$-day log return is the sum of the $h$ daily log returns, since log returns add.
The days are independent, so the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances.
Each day has variance $\sigma^2$, so the sum has variance $h\sigma^2$.
Take the square root: the standard deviation is $\sigma\sqrt{h}$.
Standard deviations add too, so the spread is $h\sigma$.
lines.why: Only variances add for independent terms. Good and bad days cancel, so the spread grows more slowly.

hints.text: Start from what an h-day return is made of.
Independent terms add variances, not standard deviations.
Variance $h\sigma^2$, then the root.

feedback.correct: Variance grows with $h$, so spread grows with $\sqrt{h}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Sum, variances add, count the days, take the root.

byKey.x: You added the standard deviations. That treats every day as moving the same way.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: The sum of $h$ independent days has variance $h\sigma^2$. Its root is $\sigma\sqrt{h}$, which gave 4.583% at 21 days.

screens.title: Profit, not error
screens.prose: A signal calls the direction of a futures contract each day. It is right 52% of the time. A typical move is 8 bp, and each trade costs 0.5 bp.
screens.question: What is the average profit per trade after costs, in bp?

hints.text: A right call wins 8 bp and a wrong call loses 8 bp.
Gross edge is 0.52 × 8 - 0.48 × 8.
That is 0.32 bp. Take off the 0.5 bp cost.

feedback.correct: -0.18 bp. A real edge, spent on costs.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the gross edge, then subtract the cost.

byKey.gross: You stopped before costs. The firm is paid after them.
byKey.mixed: You subtracted 0.5 from the 52%. Those are different units.
byKey.sign: The gross edge is 0.32 bp and the cost 0.5 bp, so 0.32 − 0.5 is below zero. A positive 0.18 takes 0.5 − 0.32, the wrong way round.

explain.text: A trading firm scores a signal by profit after costs. A 52% hit rate looks fine and loses money here, so the loss function is the P&L.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks "Which horizon, and when do you decide?" The bars show the return spread at each horizon.
screens.question: What do you answer?

options.text: One day, decided at the close, once signal and cost are known.
As long as possible, since longer horizons give a higher R squared.
options.why: Overlapping long returns inflate R² without adding skill.

options.text: Whichever horizon scores best on the full history, then fix it.
options.why: You chose the horizon on the data you score on. That is tuning on the test.

options.text: Each morning, once I have seen the open and early prices.
options.why: You moved the decision after the information. Decide when the features are fixed.

hints.text: Fix the decision time first.
The horizon should be chosen before scoring, from what you can trade.
Start with one day and lengthen it only on later data.

feedback.correct: One day, fixed at the close, and extended only on later data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose the horizon from what you can trade, not from the score.

byKey.long: You chose by R². Overlap inflates it.
byKey.best: You tuned the horizon on the full history.
byKey.open: You decided after seeing the open, so the features move.

explain.text: Fix the decision time, then the horizon. Test a longer horizon only on later data you have not tuned on.

ideas: Turn the question into a target, a horizon and a loss, and name the baseline before any model.
Model the return, not the price: a price level scores a high R² for free.
Spread grows with the square root of the horizon, and the honest loss is the money made after costs.
